slides.title: Why Treasury Yields Don't Simply Follow the Fed
lines: A story about bond prices, long-term risk and what markets already expect.
THE FED CUTS. LONG YIELDS RISE.
Why the bond market can move in the opposite direction to the central-bank headline.

slides.title: The obvious trade can be the wrong one
lines: “Rates fell. So why did my long bond lose money?”
The Fed sets a short policy rate. Investors price a long series of future outcomes.

slides.title: A bond is a promise of future cash payments
lines: Price changes because investors reassess the value of the promised cash flows.

slides.title: The basic inverse relationship
lines: At a 4% yield: $105 / 1.04 ≈ $100.96. Same payoff, higher price.
One-year bond illustration; real coupon-bearing Treasury securities require full discounting.

slides.title: Why the long end reacts more
lines: Hypothetical 7-year modified duration; yields rise 50 basis points.
First-order approximation, before convexity, spread changes and carry.

slides.title: One policy rate. Many market yields.
lines: Influences overnight funding conditions and expectations of its future policy path.
Prices years of expected short rates, inflation compensation, risk premia, supply and liquidity.
“The Fed cut” is one input to the 30-year bond price — not a sufficient explanation.

slides.title: Two components behind a long nominal yield
lines: The term premium is model-estimated, not directly quoted by an exchange.

slides.title: Term premium is useful — and uncertain
lines: Two investors can disagree on the compensation required to hold long bonds even with similar short-rate forecasts.
ACM is an estimate inferred from a model. Different methods can deliver different levels and revisions.
Never present a fitted term premium as if it were an observed Treasury quote.

slides.title: A yield curve contains many maturities
lines: Two deliberately stylised illustrative curves — not observed Treasury values.
Conceptual yield-curve shifts; vertical scale is intentionally unnumbered.
Compare a fixed-maturity Treasury curve, not arbitrarily selected bond coupons.

slides.title: Four patterns, four different mechanisms
lines: Both yields fall; shorter maturity falls more.
Both yields rise; longer maturity rises more.
Both yields fall; longer maturity falls more.
Both yields rise; shorter maturity rises more.
The labels describe curve mechanics. Growth, inflation or supply is a hypothesis to test.

slides.title: What if the front end falls while the long end rises?
lines: Hypothetical mixed-direction steepening: it need not be a textbook “bull” or “bear” shift.
2s30s widens 40bp. Do not label the macro cause from slope alone.

slides.title: Nominal versus real yields
lines: A quoted nominal par yield includes compensation linked to future purchasing power and nominal discounting.
A TIPS real yield plus a nominal-real gap gives breakeven inflation, with liquidity/risk effects.
Example: 5.0% nominal − 2.6% real ≈ 2.4% breakeven. Not a pure inflation forecast.

slides.title: Heavy issuance can complicate the story
lines: When-issued yield, stop-out, bid-to-cover and dealer allocation help assess demand at the auction.
One weak auction cannot prove a funding crisis. Compare timing, tenor, market context and historical distributions.
A 30Y sale does not tell you what happened to 5Y term premium.

slides.title: Easier Treasury yields can still mean dearer borrowing
lines: Illustrative matched-maturity change; issuer financing cost actually increases.
Always distinguish Treasury duration relief from credit-risk deterioration.

slides.title: The journey from policy to financing
lines: A disruption at any step can blunt the intended policy transmission.

slides.title: When the 30Y sells off, collect discriminating evidence
lines: Was the expected short-rate path repriced?
Did real rates, inflation compensation, or both rise?
What changed in model estimates, issuance and auctions?
Did spreads, equities and funding conditions corroborate?

slides.title: Before you move on, try three tests
lines: Yield rises 50bp; duration is 7. Approximate price?
Is term premium a directly observed Treasury price?
Long yields rise after a Fed cut. Does that prove growth optimism?
Try to answer before reading the green response.
